# Wirecard and Jan Marsalek: Evidence-Bounded Reconstruction of the Public-Fraud Trail

## Executive summary

The available evidence supports only a limited reconstruction of the Wirecard public-fraud trail. It establishes that:

- Wirecard AG publicly disclosed the results of a KPMG special investigation on 28 April 2020.
- Wirecard characterized that investigation as finding no incriminating evidence of balance-sheet forgery and no significant findings requiring adjustment of the 2016–2018 annual accounts.
- The same disclosure acknowledged that KPMG could not obtain all data it considered necessary to prove certain revenues for 2016–2018 because relevant information was primarily controlled by third parties.
- Wirecard stated that its 30 April 2020 annual-account release and annual press conference would be postponed, and that it would coordinate with EY on completing audit work.
- A November 2020 European Parliament Economic Governance Support Unit study assessed that all five identified lines of defence against corporate fraud and deception had failed “in one way or another.”
- The available source material does **not** establish the discovery or status of the purported €1.9 billion in trustee accounts, the details of EY’s audit opinions, official findings by BaFin, ESMA, APAS, FREP, prosecutors or courts, or the circumstances and present status of Jan Marsalek’s disappearance.

Accordingly, the evidence supports a documented conflict between Wirecard’s contemporaneous corporate presentation and a later policy assessment that the company’s internal and external oversight architecture had failed. It does not, from the supplied sources alone, establish the full fraud mechanism, responsibility of particular individuals, the fate of the missing cash, or Marsalek’s location.

## Scope and evidentiary standard

This report treats 1 October 2026 as the current date but uses only the two source excerpts returned by the research tools. The absence of later source material is itself significant: developments that may have occurred after the cited documents cannot be asserted here.

The sources have different evidentiary character:

- **Source 1** is a primary corporate disclosure by Wirecard AG. It records what Wirecard said about the KPMG investigation and its own financial-reporting position. It is not, by itself, independent confirmation of those assertions.
- **Source 2** is a policy study prepared for the European Parliament’s Committee on Economic and Monetary Affairs. It contains the authors’ assessment and recommendations. The study expressly states that its opinions are the authors’ responsibility and do not necessarily represent the official position of the European Parliament.

The report therefore distinguishes between:

- **Verified within the supplied record:** what the cited document itself says or records.
- **Corporate assertion:** statements made by Wirecard about its own affairs or the KPMG investigation.
- **Assessment:** conclusions expressed by the authors of the policy study.
- **Unresolved uncertainty:** matters for which the supplied sources provide no evidentiary basis.

## Chronology supported by the available evidence

### 2016–2018: Revenue verification and third-party data limitations

Wirecard stated that, during audits of its 2016–2018 annual accounts, the documents and audit procedures available at the time had been sufficient to prove revenues in its Third Party Acquiring business. This is a statement attributed to Wirecard, not an independent conclusion established by the source record. [1]

Wirecard also stated that KPMG’s enhanced forensic requirements exposed a limitation: not all data needed to prove those revenues could be obtained because the relevant data were primarily controlled by third parties. This creates an important evidentiary distinction. Wirecard presented the prior audit work as sufficient, while simultaneously acknowledging that a more demanding forensic process could not obtain all potentially necessary underlying data. [1]

### Since 2019: Internal remediation claimed by Wirecard

Wirecard stated that documentation and organizational weaknesses identified during the audit period had already been recognized internally and that the company had been addressing them since 2019. The measures it identified included establishing a Global Compliance Organization and obtaining support from external consultants. [1]

The source does not independently verify the effectiveness of those measures, the precise weaknesses involved, or whether they addressed the underlying problems later associated with Wirecard.

### December 2019: Data supplied for forensic review

Wirecard stated that it had supplied KPMG with more than 200 million data sets relating to December 2019 for forensic examination. It further stated that this examination had revealed no deviations between reported revenues and account balances. [1]

The available excerpt does not include the KPMG report itself, its methodology, the scope of the data review, or an independent assessment of Wirecard’s summary. The statement should therefore be treated as Wirecard’s characterization of the examination.

### 28 April 2020: KPMG disclosure and postponed reporting

Wirecard announced on 28 April 2020 that KPMG had delivered its special-investigation report. The disclosure was made as inside information under Article 17 of the Market Abuse Regulation and stated that the report would be published as soon as possible on Wirecard’s transparency webpage. [1]

Wirecard said that the investigation covered:

- Third Party Acquiring;
- Merchant Cash Advance and Digital Lending;
- Business activities in India; and
- Business activities in Singapore. [1]

Wirecard’s central public assertion was:

> “Incriminating evidence for the public allegations of balance sheet forgery has not been identified.” [1]

Wirecard also stated that no significant findings had been made that would require adjustment of the 2016–2018 annual accounts. [1]

At the same time, Wirecard announced that the release of its annual accounts and its annual press conference, scheduled for 30 April 2020, would not take place on that date. It said it would coordinate with EY regarding completion of audit measures, taking account of coronavirus-related restrictions and completion of the KPMG report. [1]

The combination is important but does not, without the underlying audit and forensic documents, resolve what the delay meant. The supplied sources do not establish whether the postponement resulted from unresolved audit evidence, procedural timing, logistical restrictions, or another cause.

## The audit and forensic-evidence problem

### Wirecard’s public position

Wirecard’s 28 April disclosure presented the KPMG review as not having identified incriminating evidence of balance-sheet forgery. It also stated that the December 2019 data examination found no deviations between reported revenues and account balances. [1]

Wirecard further stated that no significant findings required adjustment of the 2016–2018 accounts. [1]

These statements are evidence of what Wirecard publicly represented at the time. They are not, on the supplied record, proof that the underlying accounts were accurate or that the investigation had conclusively exonerated the company.

### Limits acknowledged in the same disclosure

The same announcement acknowledged that KPMG could not obtain all data that would have been required, under its increased forensic requirements, to prove revenues for 2016–2018. Wirecard attributed this limitation to the fact that the relevant information was primarily under third-party control. [1]

This is a central evidentiary tension:

1. Wirecard said earlier audit documents and procedures were sufficient to prove the relevant revenues.
2. KPMG’s more demanding forensic requirements could not be fully satisfied because necessary data were unavailable.
3. Wirecard nevertheless stated that no incriminating evidence of balance-sheet forgery had been identified.
4. The supplied material does not contain the full KPMG report or an independent adjudication of these propositions.

The evidence therefore does not support the stronger conclusion that the KPMG process fully verified Wirecard’s historical revenue claims.

### EY’s role remains unresolved

Wirecard’s disclosure referred to coordination with EY on completing audit measures. [1] However, the supplied source material does not provide:

- The text of EY’s 2016–2019 audit reports;
- The dates on which audit opinions were issued;
- Any qualifications, emphasis-of-matter paragraphs, disclaimers or refusals;
- The audit evidence EY obtained or could not obtain;
- Any official finding about EY’s conduct.

Those matters must remain unresolved rather than being inferred from the later collapse of Wirecard or from the policy study’s general discussion of external auditing.

## The missing €1.9 billion

The research brief specifically seeks the discovery and status of missing cash. The available source excerpts do not supply the necessary evidence.

They do not establish:

- That €1.9 billion was held in trustee accounts;
- The identity of the trustees or banks involved;
- The location of the accounts;
- Whether the balances were verified;
- When or how the alleged shortfall was discovered;
- What a Philippine banking authority concluded;
- What an insolvency administrator reported;
- Whether any court, regulator or prosecutor made a final finding concerning the money.

The only supported conclusion is therefore negative: the supplied sources do not permit a source-grounded reconstruction of the missing-cash episode. Any more detailed account would require evidence not returned by the tools.

## Regulatory and supervisory failures

### The five lines of defence

The European Parliament policy study states that, in the authors’ view, all five lines of defence against corporate fraud and deception failed “in one way or another.” It identifies those lines as:

1. Wirecard’s internal control system;
2. Wirecard’s supervisory board;
3. The external audit;
4. The oversight bodies for financial reporting and auditing; and
5. BaFin as market supervisor. [2]

The study describes the root cause as a flawed market and institutional oversight architecture and states that the architecture was not sufficiently fit to preserve market integrity and investor protection. [2]

These are the authors’ analytical conclusions. They should not be presented as a judicial or official finding because the document expressly qualifies its opinions as those of the authors rather than necessarily those of the European Parliament. [2]

### Internal controls and supervisory governance

The study recommends requiring listed companies to maintain an appropriate and effective internal-control system. It also recommends that the head of internal control report to the supervisory board rather than management, and that internal-control audits be considered. [2]

These recommendations indicate the authors’ assessment that internal-control arrangements were an important weakness exposed by the Wirecard case. They do not, on the supplied evidence, identify a particular control failure, responsible officer, or specific transaction.

### External audit

The study recommends strengthening external-auditor accountability so that auditors have stronger incentives to detect accounting manipulation and fraud. It links stronger auditor accountability to the information value of audits and the credibility of financial reporting. [2]

This supports a general assessment that external audit was part of the oversight problem. It does not establish that EY committed a specific violation or that any individual auditor knowingly participated in fraud.

### Financial-reporting oversight and BaFin

The study states that BaFin required considerably stronger supervisory and enforcement powers and recommends broad forensic and investigative powers. It also recommends making self-regulatory enforcement bodies such as FREP purely ancillary and optional. [2]

The supplied source identifies BaFin, FREP and APAS in the study’s institutional framework, but it does not provide detailed investigative findings by any of them. Consequently, the evidence supports the policy study’s criticism of the supervisory architecture, but not a detailed factual account of particular regulatory acts, omissions, warnings or enforcement decisions.

### Information flows and whistleblowing

The study recommends improving the flow of information to markets and supervisors while preserving whistleblowing and short selling as important information sources. [2]

This is a policy conclusion rather than evidence that a particular whistleblower report or short-selling allegation was correct. The supplied sources do not establish the content, timing or outcome of any such report or allegation.

## Jan Marsalek

The supplied evidence does not provide a source-grounded account of Jan Marsalek’s disappearance.

It does not establish:

- The date of his disappearance;
- His last verified location;
- His route or movements;
- Whether he left Germany voluntarily or unlawfully;
- His present location as of 1 October 2026;
- His legal status;
- Any warrant, indictment, arrest notice or court finding;
- The identity of any alleged accomplices;
- Any verified relationship between Marsalek and other persons or entities.

Therefore, no factual narrative linking Marsalek’s disappearance to the missing cash, Wirecard’s accounting, or particular third parties can be drawn from the available sources. Those subjects remain evidentiary gaps.

## What can and cannot be linked

### Supported links

The sources support the following limited chain:

1. Wirecard operated a public company reporting and audit process covering, among other matters, Third Party Acquiring revenue. [1]
2. Wirecard announced a KPMG special investigation into several business areas. [1]
3. Wirecard publicly characterized the KPMG results as not identifying incriminating evidence of balance-sheet forgery. [1]
4. Wirecard acknowledged that KPMG could not obtain all data required under enhanced forensic standards to prove certain historical revenues. [1]
5. Wirecard postponed publication of its annual accounts and annual press conference and referred to further coordination with EY. [1]
6. A later policy study assessed that the company’s internal controls, supervisory board, external audit, financial-reporting oversight and BaFin had all failed in some respect. [2]

### Unsupported links

The supplied evidence does not support linking:

- The KPMG disclosure to a verified finding about the €1.9 billion;
- The missing cash to Jan Marsalek;
- Marsalek’s disappearance to a particular escape route or accomplice;
- Any specific conduct to EY, BaFin, APAS, FREP, prosecutors or courts;
- The policy study’s assessment to a formal finding of criminal liability;
- Wirecard’s public statements to intentional deception by a named individual.

## Contradictions and evidentiary tensions

### Corporate reassurance versus incomplete forensic access

Wirecard’s disclosure stated both that no incriminating evidence of balance-sheet forgery had been identified and that not all data required to prove certain revenues under enhanced forensic standards could be obtained. [1]

These propositions are not necessarily logically incompatible: absence of identified incriminating evidence is not the same as complete verification. However, they create a material evidentiary tension. The disclosure could reassure investors while simultaneously acknowledging that the forensic process lacked some underlying information.

### Prior audit sufficiency versus enhanced forensic requirements

Wirecard stated that the documents and audit measures available during the 2016–2018 audits had been sufficient to prove revenues, but also said that KPMG’s increased requirements could not be fully met because relevant data were controlled by third parties. [1]

The sources do not explain whether this reflected a higher evidentiary standard, deficiencies in the earlier audit process, limitations in the company’s records, or another factor.

### Corporate disclosure versus broader institutional-failure assessment

Wirecard’s disclosure presented the KPMG investigation in relatively favorable terms. [1] The later policy study assessed that all five lines of defence had failed in one way or another. [2]

This is a difference in perspective and evidentiary function rather than a direct contradiction. The first source records a company statement about a particular investigation; the second offers a broad policy assessment of the scandal. Neither supplied source contains the full official record needed to determine precisely how the two should be reconciled.

## Evidentiary gaps that prevent a complete reconstruction

A complete public-fraud trail cannot be reconstructed from the supplied material because the following evidence is absent:

- Wirecard’s full 2016–2019 annual reports;
- The exact wording and status of EY audit opinions;
- The complete KPMG special-investigation report;
- Official findings concerning the purported €1.9 billion;
- Trustee-account records or banking confirmations;
- Philippine banking-authority findings;
- Insolvency-administrator reports;
- German parliamentary committee findings;
- BaFin, ESMA, APAS or FREP investigative findings;
- Prosecutorial indictments or judicial findings;
- Verified information about Marsalek’s disappearance or current status;
- Evidence of relationships among Marsalek, Wirecard personnel, trustees, banks or other entities.

The correct conclusion is therefore not that these events did not occur, but that they cannot be asserted on the basis of the returned evidence.

## Overall conclusion

The returned evidence documents the early public stage of the Wirecard crisis rather than the complete fraud trail. It shows a company publicly defending the results of a special investigation while acknowledging limits on access to underlying third-party data and delaying its annual reporting timetable. It also shows an independent policy study later treating the case as evidence of systemic failure across corporate controls, supervisory governance, external audit, financial-reporting oversight and market supervision.

The evidence does **not** establish the missing-cash facts, the ultimate status of the purported €1.9 billion, the details of any criminal conduct, or Jan Marsalek’s disappearance and present whereabouts. Those issues must remain unresolved in a responsible account limited to the returned sources.

## Sources

[1] [Wirecard AG: “KPMG delivers report on special investigation,” 28 April 2020](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation)

[2] [Katja Langenbucher, Christian Leuz, Jan Pieter Krahnen and Loriana Pelizzon: “What are the wider supervisory implications of the Wirecard case?”, European Parliament Economic Governance Support Unit, PE 651.385, November 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf)
